utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please be seated. Mr. Registrar, will you have the witness brought in? (The accused/witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I should first like to say good afternoon to our friends, interpreters, the court reporters, the Prosecution and the Defence counsel, the accused, who is our witness -- I am recalling this fact for the benefit of the public gallery -- a witness under oath like all other witnesses. May I make a few words of explanation? Mr. Registrar, there was some confusion over the beginning of this hearing, taking into consideration that one of our colleagues was in audience, so I may have made a mistake as to whether it was 2.00 or 2.30, but I see that the parties have adjusted to a Judge who has made a mistake.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: In that case, it is also my fault.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: So we only have the guilty in this courtroom now. Thank you for your understanding, I apologise once again, and we can continue now, Mr. Nobilo. I suppose you were able to make a timetable regarding the end of the examination-in-chief. Mr. Registrar has told us an evaluation. Perhaps you can tell us now in public, though you need not be committed by what you state.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: It is difficult to envisage the course of proceedings because, as you see yourself, sometime the discussion takes a particular turn, we spend more time than we had planned on it, but all this is in the interests of justice. When we came back to the days after Ahmici and all the talks that our witness had with various international agencies and all his activities in connection with the investigation over Ahmici, as we approach the end of the year, things will speed up because there are much fewer events. It is hard for me to evaluate but ... Two whole days, perhaps two and a half. That would be our estimate, two working days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I wish to tell you -- I can, I think, speak on behalf of my colleagues -- that the number of questions put by the Judges will not take this same form, so this time will be compensated in one way or another. Do you have any comments to make, Judge Shahabuddeen? Any observations? No? Judge Rodrigues? No? Mr. Nobilo, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: General, I think last week we finished sometime in April 1993, and we can now go on to the most important events as of May the 1st, 1993. So will you please, in summary form but, for the moment, leave aside the fighting and the war which is ongoing -- I think this is where Their Honours are aware of -- but within the context of those wartime events, could we focus on events that have a direct or indirect bearing on the charges against you?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, of course, Mr. Nobilo. I congratulate you. I think that is how we should approach this issue, that is, that the witness should focus on the events that are relevant for the charges against him. So please continue, Mr. Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours. On the 1st of May, 1993, I had a meeting with a member of the joint command, Mr. Franjo Nakic, who requested from me that the joint command should be filled in with three officers so that it could fully function together with representatives of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and issue joint orders and work on the implementation of the agreements that have been signed with representatives of the BH army. I also had a meeting, a regular meeting, with my associates, later on during the day with my assistant for security, and we reviewed the manifestations of disturbances of order and discipline both in HVO units and in the pocket, that is, in the Lasva River Valley. I asked for more detailed information from the assistant for security and a proposal of measures to prevent privately-organised exchanges. These exchanges were particularly intensive between the towns of Vitez and Zenica, and a very high commission was charged for this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell us, General, most of these privately-organised exchanges, what was their substance, very briefly? Anyone who organised the exchange, would he force the person leaving his place of residence to go somewhere else, or was it someone who wanted to leave Vitez or Zenica asked the organisers of the exchange to carry out the exchange?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: In most cases, the people who wished to leave Vitez which, in those days, together with Busovaca, was under siege, looked for mediators who would escort them across the front lines, at a price of course; and in the majority of cases these were exchanges due to the departure of prisoners released simultaneously, that is, Bosniak Muslims leaving from Vitez to Zenica and Croats leaving Zenica to go to Vitez. Then these released prisoners did everything they could to bring over their families as well by engaging mediators for a certain commission. Another manifestation of disruptions of order were thefts, particularly thefts of explosives, as in Vitez there was an explosives factory and these explosives were sold even on the front lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: General, let us go back a little. You said that from your assistant for security you required information and measures to prevent exchanges. Why did you wish to prevent those exchanges? What was your position regarding them?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I was guided by the positions of the UNHCR, and those were that there should be no resettlement and abandoning of homes. I didn't want those people to leave because I believed that once all the signed agreements were implemented the security situation would significantly improve and that we would manage to separate the forces, that is, the HVO and the BH army, in terms of the front line, and create conditions for the implementation of the principle of freedom of movement and for full security of each citizen living there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: On that same day, the 1st of May, 1993, you also had a meeting with a representative of the Red Cross, de la Mota, and he raised an issue regarding the prevention of freedom of movement for Muslims. Tell us how this conversation evolved.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: This meeting was a rather lengthy one with Mr. de la Mota and there were a number of agenda items discussed. A special issue was the problem of Bosniak Muslims living in Gacice, and de la Mota underlined the problem that there were Bosniak Muslims living in seven houses, that they were from Gacice, whereas the other houses were not fit for accommodation, damaged, some of them burnt, or they had been moved into by other refugees; and de la Mota stressed that the Bosniak Muslims in those seven houses were actually hostages because they did not enjoy freedom of movement. He even said that each of the Bosniak Muslims whose house had been burned in the village of Gacice or which was unfit to live in would voluntarily move to the area of Zenica or, rather, areas under the control of the BH army. Mr. de la Mota asked me to implement the principle of freedom of movement and said that the Bosniak Muslims wanted to leave Gacice to other areas under control of the BH army and that they were willing to sign a paper to that effect. At the time, I told Mr. de la Mota that his position was probably shared by the International Red Cross but that it was in contradiction with the position of the UNHCR because if Bosniak Muslims were to leave the village of Gacice, then the UNHCR would assess that as an instance of ethnic cleansing; and since they were still in the village of Gacice, Mr. de la Mota, the representative of the Red Cross, described this as not allowing them freedom of movement. As far as I can remember, this problem was later resolved in such a way that the majority of the Bosniak Muslims, escorted by the UN, left Gacice via Dubravica to Zenica, but I know that the army did not participate in that resettlement of the population. At that meeting, we also discussed the question of detained Croatian civilians; I also requested the evacuation of the wounded from the church hospital in Nova Bila; I also asked for Mr. de la Mota's assistance in taking care of the displaced who were coming on a weekly basis in large groups from Zenica to Vitez. I also mentioned the example of the disappearance of Croats in Zenica. I gave a specific example of Mr. Nenad Gelic who had gone missing from Zenica, and also some of his neighbours. I also asked for information about Mr. Zivko Totic, the commander of the Zenica Brigade, and the four officers from the Stjepan Tomasevic Brigade command in Novi Travnik. I also asked for information about private prisons in Zenica, such as the prison held by the 7th Muslim Brigade in the music school, and I inquired about the fate of Mr. Dobrica Jonjic, to see whether he was alive at all, then also I asked for information about prisoners being held in Kacuni, Tarcin, Rostovo, and I also promised that I would provide a list of casualties to Mr. de la Mota -- I'm thinking of HVO casualties -- and I asked him to also make efforts to ensure the implementation of the cease-fire agreement. That would roughly be the contents of our discussion. I also spoke with him about the need to act on the part of the joint commission, that is, that it should investigate crimes or, rather, that the International Red Cross must participate in investigating all crimes committed in the area of the Lasva River Valley. After that meeting, I received information from the intelligence service that troops were gathering at Ravno and Rostovo of the 7th Muslim Brigade and that reinforcements were being brought from Bugojno to Novi Travnik. Mr. Filip Filipovic, a member of the joint command of the armed forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina, but representing the HVO, informed me during the day that in the gas factory in Bilalovac, there were about 59 detained Croats; and in the course of the day I was informed that the joint command of the 3rd Corps and the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia would tour Pezici and Kruscica in the Vitez municipality as well as Tarcin and the Silo. Towards the end of the day, another issue was raised, and that is the passage of the convoy for Zenica and Gorazde, and the convoy for Zenica and Gradacac. Both these convoys were convoys carrying armaments and military equipment for the needs of the BH army. On the 2nd of May, 1993, I had a meeting with the command of the Vitez Brigade, and at that meeting I was told that 130 Croats had already arrived from Zenica and had settled in Donja Veceriska, and that they were trying to bring their families from Zenica to Vitez, and that they were working on exchanges of apartments and houses with Bosniak Muslims in Vitez. I was also informed about the problems of combat operations and the large length of the front, the exhaustion of personnel, and the difficulty in finding replacements with more rested soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: The appearance of exiled people from Zenica in Donja Veceriska, were they given permission from the civilian or military authorities, do you know? If you do know, did the military participate in those exchanges for the benefit of their families from Zenica?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I know that they were not given permission from the military authorities, nor did the military authority participate in those arrangements, linked to their moving in in Donja Veceriska, but I don't know whether they were given permission by the civilian authorities or not, I have no such information.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I was informed at the meeting that the heaviest fighting was in Kruscica, Vranjska, Gradina, Krcevine, Jardol, Dubravica, Nadioci, Grbavica, and, in fact, the entire northern part of the front line of the Vitez Brigade. There was also some discussion about crime and various forms of criminal activity, looting, eviction of people from homes and various other forms of violence. The perpetrators mostly were military conscripts coming from the area of Zenica, who wanted, at all costs, to resolve their vital problems and were ready to engage in illegal activities to do so. In the course of the day, I was also informed that equipment had been seized from a press team, and this was another manifestation of roadside burglaries, when certain groups would steal and then return this property after receiving compensation. I spoke to Croat civilians from Poculica who had been exiled already on the 16th from their homes, but I didn't get any information from the brigade commander about them. He briefed me by saying that this was a problem that was being dealt with by the civilian exchange commission, which was headed by Mr. Pero Skopljak. Around 18.37 and 19.00, a sniper from BH army positions in Stari Vitez opened fire on the command of the headquarters of the operational zone, that is the hotel building, and late in the evening I was also informed that the exiled Croats of Komusine, Jajce, and Kotor Varos had again been evicted from villages in the municipality of Vitez and Busovaca as a result of combat activity with the BH army in the period between the 16th and the 20th or 21st of April. On the 3rd of May, 1993, I received information from the Vitez Brigade that on some 28 kilometres of the front 1.600 soldiers were engaged, that is, mobilised conscripts, but that a major problem was the shortage of weaponry for all the soldiers. I was then also informed of the problem of the shortage of food, and during the day of the 3rd of May, I received for the first time a list from the Vitez Brigade command and a list of the 1st Battalion of the Vitez Brigade. Until then, we didn't have any lists and this, perhaps, was an indicator of the level of organisation in the Vitez Brigade. I was also informed about the soldiers who had been put out of action and about the tendency of desertion of the front in Novi Travnik. At 10.50, I had a meeting with the commander of the Frankopan Brigade of Travnik municipality, who informed me that the situation was extremely complex in their area, that they were receiving messages from their neighbours, Bosniak Muslims, to abandon their villages, and that they should have no reason to continue waiting in their homes or staying in their homes. He also said that the greatest difficulties were in the villages of Maljine, Podovi, Suhi Dol, Simule (phoen), Zume, Bukovci, Humac. In the course of the day, after this meeting with the commander of the Frankopan Brigade, I had some reports that a convoy would be passing carrying weapons and military equipment for the BH army for Tuzla, that is, the 2nd Corps, and partly for Brcko. This is the 2nd Corps of the BH army. Then the military service notified me that in the area of Zenica, under the supervision of the BH army, there were captured Croats kept in private prisons, in the barracks in Arnauti, Bilimiste, in the penitentiary at Zenica where about 640 Croats were kept under detention. Then I was informed that at the music school in Zenica there were also some captured Croats being kept, and during the military operations, about 24 Croats were killed, and 47 houses were burnt in Zenica, and the rest of them were devastated. According to the information I received from the Military Intelligence Service, altogether Croats had been evicted from about 20 villages in the upper part of Zenica, that is, to the south-west that adjoins the Travnik municipality. At 14.00, I received the information from the assistant for security that members of the military police were forcibly evicting Bosniak Muslims from the flats or their family houses in Vitez and that they were taking these flats and houses for themselves, so that some members had as many as two flats. That afternoon, on the 3rd of May, I also had a meeting with the representative of the International Red Cross. I think the person's name was Clare. Colonel Stewart was accompanying her. They told me that an understanding had been reached between the representatives of the 3rd Corps of the BH army to carry out an exchange of 9 HVO members, including abducted officers of the Stjepan Tomasevic and Zenica Brigades, and 3 journalists, that is, 12 altogether, to exchange them for Mujahedeen who were being detained at a district investigative prison in... After that first part of the meeting and the information that exchange would be governed by the International Red Cross criteria and with the mediation of the International Red Cross, Colonel Stewart said that because of the events in Ahmici, the HVO would earn a bad name. He told me on that occasion that representatives for human rights of the United Nations had been, on the 2nd of May, in Ahmici and that they were exposed to sniper fire in spite of the UNPROFOR escort and one of his soldiers had been wounded by protecting them. Fortunately, he said, his life was not in danger. I also told him that because of the ongoing fighting, the security situation in Ahmici was very bad, and it was almost impossible to enter the area because the houses in the village immediately next to the front line, that is, some ten metres away from the last house, and the forces were still in contact. Colonel Stewart said that he wanted peace to return, that is, recommend a cease-fire between the BH army and the Croat defence council, and I said that is what I wanted too. That meeting, on the 3rd of May, 1993, ended in this fashion.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: In relation to the information you received at 14.00 from CIS that military policemen were evicting Muslims from their flats, will you please tell us if on one of the following days you did something?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I organised a meeting, and you will see, according to chronology of events, when that happened. I also spoke to the military police, referring to my command, and the contact contrary to my orders regarding the attitude to housing. This was counter to my orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: On the 4th of May, the BH army attacked at the front in Busovaca, and they endangered the Busovaca-Kacuni road and the Busovaca-Kaonik road too. I had a meeting in the morning with Mr. Nakic, and I asked him to suggest to Dzemo Merdan to try, at the joint meeting, to resolve the problem of eviction of Croats from Zenica and Travnik and Bosniak Muslims from Vitez and Busovaca, as it was evident that the phenomenon was interrelated or, rather, that all bad that happened to Croats in Zenica found its reflection in the situation and that the fate of Bosniak Muslims in Vitez, and the reverse held true as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Before you proceed, I should like to show you D369. So Exhibit D369, 3rd of May, 1993. It was written by Mario Cerkez, the commander of the Vitez Brigade. It begins that: "It is forbidden for all members of HVO units to enter by force the houses and flats of families of Muslim nationality. All members of the HVO units are here by ordered immediately to move out of all forcibly occupied flats and houses, and to inform the People's Protection (library building) about their moving out." So will you please tell me, this order, was it taken at your order, with your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, it was the result of my order issued before that, and it clearly shows that some people behaved contrary to provisions of this order.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Even though chronologically it came a few days later but it, nevertheless, is related. So can we see D368, Exhibit D368, please? So this is D368 and you invite -- rather, you order your commander, the commander of the 4th military police battalion, and this is the process actually too because it is significant. "Actions contrary to the given orders and assignments, order. "On 30 May 1993, the officer on duty in the Central Bosnia Operative Zone informed me that Mr. Franjo Ramljak and Mr. Slavko Hrgic, both members of the Military Police, were expelling Muslim families by force. This was despite the order which bans such actions for which the above-named gentlemen are responsible. In order to prevent further actions that hinder the execution of orders and the correct behaviour of Military Police members in carrying out their assignments, I HEREBY ORDER 1. Conduct an investigation into this case and take disciplinary measures against the culprits in this incident. 2. Report to me explaining why, despite a number of warnings, certain members of your unit are still causing such negative occurrences instead of protecting public order, and suggest further actions to prevent such occurrences in future. 3. The deadline for execution of this order is 5 June 1993." Signed by Commander Tihomir Blaskic. General, will you please tell us the circumstances under which you issued this order and how do you see -- as the commander Operative Zone yet you have to address the matter of a concrete police in a concrete flat in a concrete incident?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, to begin with, we were completely surrounded. Fighting was still going on, and I said that the military police was a tool for the command and control, which was not under my command and control. I expected that the military police, while performing their daily tasks, would sanction individual cases of persecution, of eviction of Bosniak Muslims from their flats and implement -- do something to implement the orders I issued in this sense. However, instead of such an activity, I was faced with the phenomenon that the military police evicted Bosniak Muslims from flats and houses, and in this order, I requested that this case be investigated and that the commander take disciplinary measures. As I was not able, it was not under my jurisdiction to take disciplinary measures in person.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell me whether -- or, rather, if and did the commander of the military police refuse to act upon your orders, or did he do that, but then what did you do, or what could you do?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, it depended on what happened, I would see then, but my strongest weapon was to repeat the order, that is, ordered upon order, that is, I would write, "Please be so kind as to execute the order and quote the number," and then I would repeat it, of course. I would also inform the commander of the chief of the headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: But could you replace the military police commander?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I told you no, I could not dismiss him because the command or control of the military police units were not under my jurisdiction. They could carry out my orders, but I had no competencies over them, over the military police units.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: I have some terminological problems, my colleague warns me, with commander of -- with "commander of the chief of the headquarters."

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: So far, we used the term "chief of staff."

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So we used "chief of the main staff."

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: That is the supreme commanding body of the HVO in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, the chief of staff in Mostar -- chief of staff in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: There was, I think, something else that was not quite clear. What did you think? Were the military police subordinated to you or not? Was there a difference between your view and the view of the military police commander? It was after the 63rd that was -- it was after the battle when the military police were resubordinated to you. So what did you think in the wake of the battle? Were they still resubordinated to you or not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I believe we have already addressed this question, Mr. Nobilo. I think we have discussed it. We discussed already the question of hierarchy.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, we did, in the course of the battle, during the war, but now we have approached the end of May, so maybe there is not a direct battle, and under those peacetime conditions, say, were the military police still resubordinated or perhaps only during the fighting? Only one sense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: May I interrupt to ask a question, General? I understand the position to be this, that you could issue directions to the military police warning against evictions and you could request disciplinary action to be taken by the proper authorities for any infractions of your directions but that you yourself lacked the power to pursue the matter further, you had no competence over the actual sanctioned procedure; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It is correct, Your Honour. I was not the superior to the military police. I could only ask them to do certain things, that is, to implement some of my requests.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: What I want to ask is this: Do you have any knowledge to give to the Trial Chamber as to whether any sanctions were ever imposed by the proper authorities for any infractions of your directions that there were to be no evictions?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Your Honour, do you mean by the command of the military police, for instance?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: By anyone who happened to be the proper authority to impose sanctions.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, they were pronounced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: They were pronounced. Some cases? How many cases?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It is difficult to be accurate about that, but sanctions for such offences or any other offences were pronounced, and in the latter half of 1993, summary records were kept on them, that is, we had the summary of discipline measures pronounced for such and similar offences.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: What kind of disciplinary measures were pronounced?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, the mildest one was admonition, then military detention of three days, seven days, fifteen days, thirty days, and a maximum of sixty days of military detention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I wonder whether I have been as clear as I should have been. I didn't want to know what were the maximum punishments which were possible, I was asking -- or, rather, I intended to ask what kinds of punishment were, in fact, administered?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Punishment by military detention and the punishment of admonition; those were disciplinary forms of punishment. Punishment for crimes pronounced by the district military court, I have no information about that, but I do know that for a while, the district military court worked, but they conducted criminal cases rather than disciplinary infractions or offences.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Let me try a little more -- I acknowledge that the fault is entirely on my side. Were there any infractions of these directions which you issued against eviction of people? Were there any infractions, any breaches?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, there were, and there were actions which were contrary to my orders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: What I'm asking about is this: Were any punishments imposed for those infractions and, if so, what kinds of punishment were, in fact, imposed for those infractions?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not sure I understood you properly. You mean the infraction, as in infraction, actions contrary to my orders?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: That's right. Were people sent to gaol --

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: You mean in this specific case, the military police commander?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, never, because I had no jurisdiction over him. I was not his superior and I could not take any measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I understand you very well. You couldn't send the police commander to gaol; you could report that there were certain breaches of your instructions and you could ask that the military police disciplinary procedures be activated. After that I understand you to be saying the matter was out of your hands. What I'm asking, General, is this: Were there, in fact, any cases in which anyone was, in fact, punished for violating your orders that there were to be no infractions, no evictions, and, if so, what kinds of punishment were meted out to those people? Were they admonished? Were they sent to gaol?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Instances of their being in gaol, I do not -- no, not to my knowledge, but there were certain measures that were taken of particular duties. Perhaps you will see later from the chronology. Not only in this particular case but in relation to all other actions, I wrote to the commander, to the chief of staff, and asked him to intercede and see that these people are taken off duty. Unfortunately, this did not take place automatically but it did eventually happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Mr. Nobilo, I apologise for interrupting you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Perhaps it is now time to make a short break. Thank you. A quarter of an hour break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The hearing is resumed. Please be seated. Mr. Nobilo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: General, before the break, in answer to a question by His Honour Judge Shahabuddeen, you said that some persons were dismissed from duty, that you had requested this from the chief of staff but, unfortunately, this did not happen automatically but it did happen eventually. So could you tell us, whose dismissal did you request and why did you consider this to be important for your Operational Zone and when did this happen?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I intervened with the chief of staff of the main staff, that he replace the commander of the military police, and that he change the organisational structure of the military police, which I considered to be wrong, and that he reorganise the military police in the Central Bosnia Operative Zone as a whole. The replacement of the commander of the military police happened about the 4th of August, 1993, and after the 4th of August, the entire command structure of the military police was changed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Excuse me. I didn't quite understand. When did you ask for this replacement? When did you make the request? I think that is what Mr. Nobilo asked you. When did you make the request for the replacement? I beg your pardon. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Mr. President, the replacement occurred on the 4th of August, 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: No, but the question was: When did you ask for this replacement? When did you ask for the replacement?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I asked for the replacement to take place, at a meeting with the chief of staff of the main staff on the 30th of April, 1993, then again on the 29th of May, 1993, and on the 10th of June, 1993. I insisted on the replacement of the commander, but I also insisted on a change of the total command structure of the military police, on its reorganisation and a change of the system of control and command within the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: We will be discussing that in detail later but, tell us, at this moment when the commander of the military police was changed, did you manage to get authority to command the military police in the Lasva River Valley?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I managed that with the new commander, Mr. Marinko Palavra who was appointed the commander of the 4th Military Police Battalion, and I acquired authority to command the military police during the period we were surrounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Were there any important personnel changes in the military police personnel?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Not only were there personnel changes, but the whole command structure of the military police was changed, and we embarked, step by step, upon the reorganisation of the military police. That was one of my key duties, and I was personally involved in the training of the new commanders of the companies, the military policemen, and the organisation of the military police as a whole.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you. We will go into details later, but now I have another question for you. Document D368, we see a direct command to the commander of the 4th Military Police Battalion, Pasko Ljubicic, and in this order you draw attention to negative tendencies in the military police and request changes. I should like to know what was the reason for this, the reason why, correction, after the event in Ahmici you did not also, in writing, issue a command to Pasko Ljubicic, or why didn't you call him to report to you and tell him, "Why did you give me false reports as to what you did in Ahmici?" Why didn't you do that? Could you explain that to Their Honours?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Personally, I thought that such a step would be naive on my part because upon receipt of the letter from Colonel Stewart, I became aware that this commander was sending me false reports throughout and that just to confront him with the facts would caution the commander of the military police, which would make it possible for him to take measures to make difficult any investigation or even to prevent an investigation into the crimes in Ahmici. This was a crime that I had publicly condemned and this was the first time that we witnessed such a tragedy of that proportion. Therefore, the investigation had to be at the highest possible level and it would have to involve also a break-up of the command structure of the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Why did you feel that that command structure of the military police needed to be broken up within the context of the investigation into the crime in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Precisely because I'm confident that if the same command structure were to remain, ties of solidarity would be strengthened among the members of the military police, and probably the same hierarchy within the police would have been retained, and this would have only encumbered and even made impossible the conduct of investigations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I have a little problem, General Blaskic. We're talking about Exhibit D368. We're talking about the 31st of May, 1993, and the events in Ahmici occurred on the 16th of April. I don't quite understand. You said that you would have been naive, but don't you think it was also naive on your part to ask somebody you didn't trust, that is, the commander of the 4th Military Police Battalion, to investigate evictions, whereas for several weeks you have a great deal of distrust towards this commander? We're not talking any more about the Ahmici investigation. I don't know whether you even mentioned it at the meeting of the 3rd May. We're now on the 31st of May, and we are discussing an investigation on evictions. But you are, after all, not naive. You knew that the commander of the Military Police Battalion was somebody who was involved, at least as a commander, in the event in Ahmici. How would you not be naive in sending this order and be naive if you had sent another order? What is the naivetes in this?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Mr. President, I sent this order to the commander of the military police but also to the assistant for security who had to have this order in mind, and who would supervise the reaction of the military police commander. I tried to affect a replacement of the military police commander, among other things, by sending orders of this kind and gauging the reaction to them. So after all, this was a disciplinary infraction on the part of his soldiers, but my message was that he was acting contrary to my orders. In my efforts to have him replaced, I went step by step.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I understand and it is normal for you to have had a plan, but here you have sent an order to the 4th Military Police Battalion on organised expulsions by two individuals, Ramljak and Hrgic. The date is the 31st of May. Did you make a written report to the commander of the 4th Military Police Battalion in Ahmici, because after all, it's been a month and a half since those events in Ahmici. It seems to me that I would have sent a much firmer, clear-cut order. There's Ahmici, there's expulsions, there's this, and there's that, "a meeting tomorrow in my office." I appreciate your position, but one is a bit astonished. You're not obliged to answer. I understand your strategy, but we must admit that certain questions do arise. This is six weeks after Ahmici. You yourself say that it is a major crime. The International Community is horrified by what it has learned. Colonel Stewart, whom you met on the 3rd of May, you don't even mention Ahmici again, according to my notes, and then you write a little letter to the commander of the 4th Military Police Battalion saying, "You see, you have two individuals who are not acting properly and mistreating Muslims. Make an inquiry, submit a report," and so on. I won't say any more, but it's because you spoke about naivetes. You said you would have been naive to have done otherwise. So my question is: Wasn't it naive to do this? But I think Judge Rodrigues has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I take advantage of this interruption to ask you a question, General Blaskic. You said that after some time you became aware that this commander was sending you false reports; yes?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: My question is the following: Did you, at the time, know the reasons or do you now know the reasons why this commander was sending you false reports because we are talking here about false reports, not reports that are lacking and incomplete, you are talking about false reports? Why at the time and why now, after the knowledge that you now have?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I didn't know until I was confronted with Colonel Stewart's letter, I was not aware that I was receiving false reports until then. When I read the letter by Colonel Stewart, I became aware that I was being misled and that I was receiving false reports. But what the motive of that commander was, what the background was to all this, I don't know, but I became aware that he was sending me false reports, and I thought to myself: If I were to call him and tell him, "Look, here's Colonel Stewart's report, here is your report," in that case I would have made even more difficult, or even prevented, an investigation knowing that I had no jurisdiction over the control and command of his units because it was not a question of just one individual but a unit of which he was the commander independently from me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: General, allow me to go back to the question. Certainly you became aware of that. This situation became a very serious situation for you.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It was serious and tragic and perhaps the worst situation for me, and I became aware of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Yes, I agree, but at least did you yourself ask yourself: Why is this person doing this to me?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I did try to ask myself what was the reason and why this was happening, why this had happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Yes, but in your thoughts, in your reasoning, did you have any hypothesis at least, any assumptions to explain this?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: On the 27th of April, at the press conference, I said publicly that this was a crime that had been planned, that had been organised, and that was carried out under somebody's control, and I was indeed interested to find out not only who the perpetrators were but what was at the root of this crime, and it did not occur to me that the command of the military police could have been the one who had planned it. The entire background was not clear to me nor any links that may have existed between the commander of the military police, myself, and any other authority.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: But, General Blaskic, let me go back to my question: Did you find any hypothetical explanations for the false reports that this commander was sending you?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: On the basis of my knowledge at the time and of what I know now, I believe that either he himself was aware of the tragedy and didn't have the courage to report to me about it or he believed in protecting certain people in authority who were more powerful than me and who were closer to him. I really have no other explanation what could have prompted him to send me false reports or, rather, not to inform me about what had happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: I don't want to induce your answers, but what about this hypothesis, that this commander was against your command or perhaps that he had objectives that differed from your objectives? Have you understood my question?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I -- I didn't quite understand the translation I received. Perhaps it is the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: My question is, as I have said, that I'm not going to put any explanations in your mouth, so I leave open all possible hypotheses. But what would you say with regard to this hypothesis: (1) This commander was opposed to your position as commander. He did not agree that General Blaskic should be the commander of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone; perhaps he wanted to see somebody else in that position or something of that kind. The second hypothesis: He had objectives that differed entirely from the objectives that you pursued, that you put in your orders, that you expressed in various ways of communication. So it was a personal matter, he was opposed to you, or a more substantial reason, he was against your policies. What do you think about these hypotheses? Have you understood my question now?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Yes, I did understand your question. It is difficult for me to say whether he was against me personally. I did not see any reason why this commander should be against me, why he should dislike me, but whether he was against my convictions, be that as it may, I always condemned such misdeeds and I never -- I mean, I could really never dream that anything like the crime in Ahmici could ever happen. It is difficult for me to judge him, but he was against my convictions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you, General Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I should like to turn to the Defence. I do not have a question for the witness because I do not want to embarrass him and I do not think that we should do it here before the Tribunal, and I should also like to reassure you, Mr. Nobilo and Mr. Hayman, that I should really like to know if it is the official thesis of the Defence to consider that the Ahmici massacre was organised by the commander of the military police battalion with the complicity, more or less, of somebody who was above General Blaskic. Let me repeat this. Let me do this: Mr. Blaskic does not talk about Ahmici at present and he -- and he is saying that it was a systematically planned operation. I don't know whether -- are you having any difficulties with the --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: One thing I don't understand, Mr. President. It was interpreted as "Mr. Blaskic does not talk about Ahmici at present." I don't understand what you mean. We've been talking about it for weeks, if not years.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: No, no, no. No, no, no, no. No, no, no. No, please. It is a problem which arises both for the Prosecution and for the Defence. I did not want to embarrass the accused because he is now our witness, but I have noted that for several days -- and I am trying to speak slowly -- and especially this afternoon, we are talking about Ahmici, and we find that Ahmici was programmed, planned -- not by the accused, naturally -- that the accused finds it is a crime, but now we say -- we find that it is the commander of the military police battalion, and our witness is also saying, at least he answered Judge Rodrigues that perhaps he was conniving with some higher echelons. Now, my question, and perhaps I don't expect an answer either from the Prosecution or from the Defence, but as a Judge I am entitled to ask it, and that is whether the commander of the military police battalion has been indicted by this Tribunal. Gentlemen, you do not have to answer today, of course. Now I turn to the Defence. In your system of defence, are you now affirming the idea -- at this point at which we are now -- that the Ahmici massacre was planned by some HVO elements which were of the military police, HVO police. You do not have to answer this question now, you may wait, but after all that we heard today, I simply cannot but interfere because we are talking about this and we shall now hear that Mr. -- I can't remember his name, that he programmed the massacre in Ahmici and so on and so forth. So I am not asking you to answer me today, either the Prosecution or you, the Defence, but I believe that my colleagues also share my view to ask this question because we are now in a public session and we see an interpretation which seems to make it clear to everybody because in -- Ahmici happened because we had the military police here, and the military police commander had also his superior. I am turning therefore to the Prosecutor to ask them regarding their strategy and also I am posing this question too. As I said, you do not have to answer it now, but will you please think about that?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: I would like to answer the question in private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. We are going into private session. (Private session)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Open session)

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you. We must now go back to the testimony of General Blaskic. The question was why he didn't call Pasko Ljubicic after hearing from Colonel Stewart about the crime in Ahmici. Among other things, he said that that would have been naive, that the entire command structure needs to be broken up --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, counsel. I don't think there's any need for counsel to recite the testimony that was before the Court, unless counsel, of course, has another question in this regard. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: A half an hour has gone by in the meantime, so I thought it necessary to focus on the point which we had reached before the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Nobilo, trust the Judges. They will not lose the thread in half an hour. If so, they would have long since lost the thread of the trial in view of the 22 months that we have been working. So please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: General, did you have any competencies, very briefly, to go to the police, military police, and break up their command structure?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. In my letter, when I wrote it on the 23rd, to Colonel Stewart and in all the subsequent discussions with representatives of the International Community, I sought assistance in carrying out the investigation, hoping that the international institutions at the highest level, as well as representatives of the BH army and the HVO, would join in this investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Why are you seeking assistance from the top leadership of the HVO, the BH army, and international institutions? Why did you need assistance in the investigation in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I asked for assistance because I knew that on my own I do not have the necessary strength to carry out a comprehensive investigation. When I say "investigation," I mean to identify the perpetrators as well as those who had planned and organised the whole operation. I was not competent to break up the command structure, but nor did I have the actual power to carry such a thing out within the military police, to replace the commander of the military police, to arrest 20 or 30 military policemen, to interrogate them and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What did you ask the top leadership of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna in terms of the way you thought the investigation should have been carried out?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I was assisted by the suggestion made by Colonel Stewart, and I accepted his idea, and I put it down in my written report, that the military and political leadership should be in Vitez, and that this would give momentum and support to the work of the investigating commission. I thought that a joint investigating commission, when I say "joint," I mean with representatives of both the BH army and the HVO, should be of the highest level and should have comprehensive powers. That means that it could be able to dismiss any commander on the spot, within the military police structure, who may have in any way -- who may in any way be suspected, or even if he concealed knowledge about the impending crime and, of course, it should have the right to arrest all the perpetrators. I thought it particularly important that representatives of the BH army should participate, so that investigation could be complete with regard to the soldiers and civilians who were already in the area under the control of the BH army, and the results of the investigation would have been more convincing and more complete if representatives of the BH army had participated together with the highest representatives of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did anyone that you addressed for assistance, that is the BH army, UNPROFOR, the European Monitors, the political and military leadership of Herceg-Bosna, did any one of those give you assistance in the investigation in Ahmici in 1993?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. I was left on my own, confronted with three, for me, most important problems at the time, and those were the investigation; two, measures to prevent a repetition of crime; and three, defence of biological survival in an area in which we were totally encircled and in which the forces of the BH army were eight to ten times more powerful in personnel and in terms of weaponry as compared to us in the enclave. This enclave was between one and six kilometres wide, and its maximum length was 10 to 12 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: How do you interpret the fact that the BH army did not show interest in the crimes in Ahmici in the sense of investigating those crimes in 1993? How do you interpret that? Up to perhaps a hundred Bosniaks were killed there.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: This is a question I have given thought to myself, because not at a single of the numerous meetings of the joint command did anybody insist on discovering and identifying the perpetrators of the crimes in Ahmici. I personally believe that the crime in Ahmici was a good reason for the top leadership of the BH army to launch operations to conquer Croatian territories in Travnik, Novi Travnik, Bugojno, Fojnica, Kakanj, Vares, and Zepce but, unfortunately, the crime in Ahmici also served as a motive for revenge among members of the BH army, so that there were a series of crimes that occurred in Bikosi, Maljine, Miletici, Krizancevo Selo, Buhine Kuce, Kiseljak near Zepce, Grmace in Kakanj, Gornja Zenica, Fojnica, Ostruznica, and partly in Novi Travnik, the village of Rostovci. Your Honours, Judge Shahabuddeen has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: General, do forgive me. You may have said this before and I may have missed a thread. On the 16th of April, were the military police attached to you?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: As of 11.42, it was -- they were attached to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: That means as of 11.42, Pasko Ljubicic was within your command?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: He was attached to me because of the all-out attack, but the time of that attachment or resubordination was interpreted differently but nothing changed in terms of the structure. He continued to be directly subordinate to the police administration, but temporarily he was resubordinated to me as of 11.42.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, General, you have described the occurrences at Ahmici as crimes, and they were the subject of writings in the media; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: You had a proper concern in the matter.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, when did you first discover that Pasko Ljubicic was sending you false reports?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I established that when I received the letter from Colonel Stewart on the 22nd of April, the 22nd of April, 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Now, within your military training, would you regard it as a serious matter if, on a serious question, false reports were submitted to you?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I would consider it a serious matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Would you normally institute disciplinary measures against the person submitting a false report to you on a serious matter?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, if the person is within my structure or, rather, if I am competent for instituting such measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I understand that. Now, did you either institute any disciplinary measures against Pasko Ljubicic for submitting false reports to you on a serious matter or, if you felt you did not yourself have the competence to institute disciplinary measures against him, did you request the proper authorities to institute disciplinary measures against him?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I informed my superiors about everything I learnt on the 22nd of April, and in my letter of the 23rd to Stewart -- actually, before that, I contacted the chief of staff of the main staff and asked that the commander be replaced because this was a grave criminal offence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: So your reaction was to request his replacement?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Did you ask for that in writing?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: At one point in time, in writing as well, but I requested that orally, in oral reports, when I had the occasion, and also in writing. I made the request for the replacement of the commander and for the disbanding of the military police as a whole.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Shall we have the break now? Shall we have the break now? Do you think this is a good time? Yes. We will have a 15-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The session is resumed. We shall continue until 6.00, if that is all right with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: General, you said that the B and H army was not interested in conducting an investigation in Ahmici. Will you please tell us, in all those negotiations, which were frequent after the conflict on the 16th of April, 1993, did the representatives of the BH army propose an investigation? Did they inquire about an investigation? Did they ever talk about the need to punish those who perpetrated crimes in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, they did not. We had a number of joint meetings of the joint command representatives of the BH army and the HVO and a daily matter in the town of Travnik, and even the joint command did not go to the area of Ahmici nor were there any requests for investigation or participation in an investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: If you remember the work of the joint commission for Busovaca after the January case and the Travnik commission after the Travnik conflict, how then would you explain it that earlier they went together to all scenes of conflict, into every village in Kiseljak or Busovaca, whenever a house was set on fire, Croat or Muslim, and then such a major crime and yet not once voiced an interest in going to Ahmici. Could you please explain that?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I already said that the crime in Ahmici served as a reason for broader operations by BH army in which they tried to get hold of the whole area of the Lasva Valley and Central Bosnia and, as a priority, the explosives factory and to gain control over communications and create a compact territory that would include the areas of the Central Bosnia Operative Zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Will you please describe to the Court, if the BH army had conquered the Lasva Valley, what would they be able to establish links with?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, they would have established a link between the Tuzla region, with the Zenica and Travnik region, that is, parts of east Bosnia, which were already controlled by the BH army, in Central Bosnia, and in the south, all the way to the southern part of Mostar. So forces of the 1st Corps, the forces of the 2nd Corps from Tuzla, the 3rd Corps from Zenica, the 4th Corps from Mostar, the 6th Corps from Konjic and Fojnica, and the 7th Corps from Travnik, it makes about 200.000 maybe 210.000 soldiers of the BH army which would all be connected in one compact territory with the exception of the exit to the south because the BH army had the command of the 4th Corps in Mostar down there to the south, rather, between Mostar and Caplijna.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell me, UNPROFOR, they accepted your suggestions regarding joint investigation. What did UNPROFOR focus in this way? Assistance in the investigation or something else?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: From what I could observe at the time, UNPROFOR focused on a unilateral media presentation of the crime in Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You say "unilateral media presentation." What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, I mean that they invited journalists, that they participated in giving interviews, that they were taken to places where the victims, Bosniak Muslims were, but unfortunately, they either did not want to see or hear, even though I wrote and sent information to that effect, but there was not an equitable distribution envisaged in places where Croats were victimised.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Why was it important for you that those places where Croats were victimised be shown? To justify the crime in Ahmici or why?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I did not think that a crime can be justified by a crime on the other side, and that was not in my interest at all. I wanted -- that is, I was aware, I realised that a certain adverse reaction was being created, indignation among people who lived, surrounded completely, in the Lasva Valley, among honest people and among honest HVO soldiers, were aware of that unilateral approach, and by creating this indignation, such an approach also made it more difficult for me to enlist the support of the public in conducting the investigation. My command authority, which was limited anyway, was further limited by this fact, that is, I lacked the public support. Such an action, when only the victims on one side are presented unilaterally, evidently benefited the extremist part, and they maybe wanted the crime to be forgotten or hushed up.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: General, were you given efficient and expedient help from the leadership to investigate the crime in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: After I presented and submitted a file with all documents and after I informed the leadership, I was verbally helped. It did not produce much effect. I remained most of all alone with my command, faced with the duty to conduct an investigation and to fight for their survival and also with a duty to prevent a repetition of the crime that happened in Ahmici. Apart from the verbal support, at that time I received no other form of help.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So in a situation when you were left alone, all those who took part in the investigation, in the solution, such as the international factor, the leadership of the HDZ and everybody else, they all stayed aside and you were left alone. What happened then? Will you please explain it to the Court and why?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: In that situation, I decided to launch an investigation to hire the security service which were then through investigation by a secret --

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You said security service. You mean -- you mean ... Shall we define who was to conduct the investigation? Will you give us the full title and the authority of the service?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It is the Information and Security Service which also had control over the military police and with whose help I intended to collect evidence which would then serve to prompt the military and political leadership of Herceg-Bosna to join in the investigation of the crime in Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So you asked the information and security service. The acronym is SIS?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What did you expect from them? What were they supposed to hand over to you?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: They were to give me evidence that I would use to prompt the arrival of a commission from the very top of the Croat community of Herceg-Bosna, which would then conduct a complete investigation on the site.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us go back to the period of time where we were before we made this digression, where you explained why you did not call Pasko Ljubicic immediately after you received from Colonel Stewart information about Ahmici. Will you please tell us, as of the 4th of May onward, which were the key talks which representatives of the International Community about Ahmici and what did you meet with them about?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: On the 4th of May at 15.00, I was off to attend a meeting that was taking place in the neighbouring office where Mr. Thebault was present, he was the head of the European Observer Mission for the region of Zenica, Colonel Stewart. There were also other members of the European Observer Mission, but I do not know their names as I did not know these persons and they did not participate in a discussion. The meeting took place in the office of Ante Valenta, who was temporarily staying at the Vitez Hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Will you please tell the Court who Ante Valenta was? What was his office and what was the relationship between you and Ante Valenta?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: As far as I know, Ante Valenta was a coordinator in the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, responsible for the Central Bosnian region, and he had his office in Travnik. Until the 8th of April, 1993, and after the incidents broke out between the HVO and the BH army of 8 April, he temporarily used the office of the chief of staff, Mr. Franjo Nakic, in the Vitez Hotel, and between me and Ante Valenta, there were no official or any kind of hierarchical relationship.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Will you please -- then the question is: What was the most important thing said at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Immediately after I entered, I guess the meeting was ready and away, Colonel Stewart turned to me and asked me, "Who ordered to kill civilians in Ahmici?" I told Colonel Stewart, "I did not. It was not under my command and these are not my units." Colonel Stewart said after that, for the commission of genocide in Ahmici, the Vitez authorities will be accused. He said that his soldiers had seen HVO soldiers, they secured Muslims in Ahmici. After that, he picked up a blue folder and said, "You see? I have the names of perpetrators of the crimes, and I shall turn over these names to Mr. Ambassador." He meant Mr. Thebault, the head of the European Observer Mission. He also, I mean Colonel Stewart, emphasised also, "I have names here on the list. The survivors know who they were attacked by, and the authorities in Vitez bear the responsibility for the rehabilitation of that place." "The mission, which is investigating the crimes, from the United Nations will visit all the villages. The mission has not yet arrived at clear results and facts, but this is a crime," Colonel Stewart said. Immediately after Colonel Stewart, the floor was taken by Mr. Thebault, the head of the European Observer Mission, who said, "You must investigate what happened as soon as possible, because so far it has been discovered that five people, five persons, had been burnt, and if it is established that more people were killed then it is a deliberate crime. You must see to it." That's what he said to me, Mr. Thebault, I mean, "You must ensure the freedom of movement for civilians, their protection, and the protection of their right to life." After that, the floor was taken by Mr. Valenta and he said the following: "The people are frustrated. The collapse of public law and order and safety has taken place. Serbs are procrastinating with implementation of the Vance-Owen plan and the activities regarding the implementation of the plan, if the Serbs sign it or if they do not sign it, will be quite opposite. The BH army and the Muslim forces are terrorising Croats, and the BH army has territorial pretences to the Lebensraum, the living space, of the Croats. We are completely surrounded." When I was given the floor I told those gentlemen the following: "I need help to investigate the crime, and the commission must be of a mixed composition in order to arrive at objective results. I request that it be representatives of the HVO, of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, European Monitoring Mission, UNPROFOR, and the International Red Cross. The British Battalion needs to assist both when going into or leaving Ahmici and in providing security conditions." I also said that we first had to separate the forces of the BH army and the HVO in keeping with the agreement signed on the 21st of April, 1993, and we also needed to provide the conditions for UNPROFOR patrols, and only then would we be able to have sufficient security for the movement of civilians and building of renewed trust and confidence between the Muslim and the Croat people.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did he say something about fears that crimes such as the one in Ahmici might be repeated?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: He only emphasised -- as a matter of fact, before Thebault stepped in, I also said that the security situation was very complex because we were surrounded, and Thebault said that Celebici and Ostrosac are major problems for humanitarian missions, and what happened in Vitez, in Ahmici, may not be repeated. He repeated it once again, "Ahmici may not happen again."

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: General, your first statement was, when you were asked who ordered to murder civilians in Ahmici, you said, "Not me nor my units." Did you lie to Stewart and Thebault or did you tell them the truth?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I told them the truth, because we always, and that is how I was brought up and trained, we called "our" units the units directly subordinated to me. That was the principle in the secondary military school at the military academy and whilst I was with the JNA. We always called "my" units those units which were under our direct command that were directly subordinate to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Judge Shahabuddeen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: General, I understand the distinction you are making between units which were directly answerable to you and the other HVO type units which were not answerable to you. Did you, at the time, think that your interlocutors understood this distinction, that they understood that there might be HVO units that are were not legally answerable to you, or did you have the impression that they understood that all of the HVO units were under your command?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Your Honour, I had quite a number of meetings with Colonel Stewart, and I am deeply convinced that he understood what I was saying, because I tried to explain to him what the HVO actually was and that it was still the armed people. I don't wish to repeat myself as to the explanations I gave. I think he understood me. However, the situation at the time was such that I myself was confronted with the problem of the investigation, and perhaps it would not have been prudent on my part if I had come out openly and told him, "Members of the military police are suspected for this," and if then the next day such a report would appear in the media, which I believed he would have done, and this would have had a disastrous effect, I think, not only for me personally but also for the command, which that same military police was securing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: General, did you, at the time, think that Colonel Stewart was understanding you to mean that it was the military police who were responsible, but that you were taking the position that the military police were not answerable to you?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I believe that he understood when I said that it hadn't been done by my units, but I wouldn't be so bold as to claim that he understood who I meant from what I said, that is, when I said, "Not my units."

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell us openly here at this trial, you are on trial and perhaps we don't have to be so cautious, how did Bob Stewart operate after Ahmici? What methods did he use? How did he work?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: From Ahmici on, I got to know another Bob Stewart. For me, it was not the same man that I had known until Ahmici when it comes to his attitude towards the HVO. I can, up to a point, understand that he himself was distressed by what he saw in Ahmici, but he generalised the problem of Ahmici to implicate the whole HVO, and in his activities he used the media, and he gave emphasis to that problem. I'm more than a hundred per cent sure that he would have used the media to place any other information, if I had given them to him, when I was left on my own facing the need to conduct an investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: When you said and Bob Stewart repeated on the CNN that the military police had committed the crime in Ahmici, if you had done that, what do you think would have happened in such a situation? What would have happened to you and the whole enclave?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I'm confident that a reaction would have ensued, probably by those same members, which would have had serious consequences. I think that is clear and understandable.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell us, how did the meeting with Colonel Stewart end, Colonel Stewart and Ambassador Thebault?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The meeting ended -- actually, I noticed, while I was speaking, that Colonel Stewart was taking notes. Colonel Stewart had a blue diary, like an ordinary notebook, and Mr. Thebault had a similar one, and they were taking note of our comments. Towards the end of the meeting, I received a report on the grouping of BH army forces in the broad area north of the Vitez, the village of Janjac, and after I received that report we parted without having reached any concrete conclusions, and as no one spoke after I had suggested the formation of a joint commission, I had expected a reaction to my proposal to form such a joint commission, the more so as I had repeated at the time that because of the greater weight of the results and in order to create the best possible conditions for the investigation, a joint commission would be far more successful.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: On that same day, later on, about 18.00 hours, de la Mota came. Can you tell us what you discussed with de la Mota?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Mr. de la Mota told me that there were further cases of persecution of Muslims in areas under HVO control.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Could you please tell us which organisation Mr. de la Mota belonged to?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I think he was the representative of the International Red Cross, but I need to check that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: According to your recollection, tell us, what did you discuss?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: He told me explicitly that extremist HVO forces were acting, and he mentioned the case of the expelling of Nihada Sivro, a Bosniak Muslim family from Podgradina, and apparently the house had been looted and the family had been thrown out and moved to the elementary school in Vitez. I later gave orders for an investigation into the case, and I established that this incident had been provoked by members of the Vitezovi special purpose unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: When you received that information, let us follow the chronology, did you react? Did you take any measures when you realised that the Vitezovi were the culprits?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I requested an investigation be conducted; however, though I was told that the Vitezovi were behind this incident, I was not given the actual names of the perpetrators because the Vitezovi unit retained its status of direct communication with the defence department.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did you tell Darko Kraljevic that one of his men may have done it?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I told him that I had heard that and that his behaviour was contrary to the orders I had issued prohibiting persecution and expelling of Bosniak Muslims from Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did he promise an investigation or did he refuse to cooperate?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: He promised he would take measures, but he didn't inform me as to whether he had taken any measures or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Let us go back to the meeting with Mr. de la Mota.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Mr. de la Mota also pointed out that in front of the British battalion camp in Nova Bila, there were Bosniak Muslim families who had been exiled from Jajce and who had previously been accommodated in the Divjak neighbourhood, Vitez municipality, and de la Mota said again that HVO extremists were in action and that they had exiled these Bosniak Muslim families to the area of the UN compound.
