I told Mr. de la Mota that I had issued an order prohibiting persecution of Muslims, and I said to Mr. de la Mota that it would be far easier to improve the security situation if we were to separate the BH army forces from the HVO forces on the front lines, and if we were to implement the agreement of the 21st of April, 1993, thereby the conditions would be created for the freedom of movement and for the security of citizens.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell us, did de la Mota notice the difference between your positions and the positions held by some other people in power in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. When I spoke about these matters, such as freedom of movement and security for the entire population living in the Lasva River Valley, de la Mota said to me that my stances were contrary to the positions held by Mr. Valenta, and I responded to Mr. de la Mota that Mr. Valenta was a representative of the civilian authorities and that he was only temporarily staying in Vitez because he couldn't go back to Travnik and that he does not have any functions in the town of Vitez -- I meant no military functions -- and also at the level of the municipality, I knew that he didn't have any civilian functions. After that, Mr. de la Mota told me that the situation was extremely complicated and confusing, the media were heightening tension, which certainly did not contribute to an overall settlement.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Could you summarise, in two or three sentences, where did Mr. de la Mota notice the differences between your positions and those of Mr. Valenta? What was the difference?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I told Mr. de la Mota that I didn't see any problems in coexistence in the Lasva River Valley in any sense except for security because the enclave is very small and the front lines are sometimes only one kilometre to the north and the south of the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Coexistence between whom?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Between the Muslims and Croats in this area of the Operative Zone of Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So you felt you could live together, Muslims and Croats. What was the position of Mr. Valenta? The answer wasn't interpreted. You believe that Croats and Muslims could live together; is that true?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What was the position of Mr. Valenta, according to Mr. de la Mota?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Mr. de la Mota told me that Mr. Valenta held the opposite view.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: How did you understand that? What was Mr. Valenta's position, if it was opposite to yours?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I assume and believe that he advocated separation of areas, that the Croats should live in one area and the Muslims in another area.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: During the day of the 4th and the 5th, I also had a meeting with Mr. Akhavan, and he wanted me to tell him what had happened on the 16th of April, 1993, and briefly I described the events of the 16th of April, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. Akhavan, how did he introduce himself? In what capacity had he come to Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't have a note of his position, so I cannot recollect exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Was that the same person that testified here as a witness?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: After I briefly described the events, Mr. Akhavan said, "Your units, on your orders, carried out the massacre in Ahmici and killed civilians." My answer to Mr. Akhavan was that they hadn't committed a crime under my orders because I hadn't ordered the commission of a crime and I know for certain that my units had not done that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Was Akhavan familiar with the situation in Central Bosnia? Was this the first time that he appeared?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Excuse me. Every time, when you ask this question, Mr. Blaskic, you're not astonished to see that the same question is being asked of you, that you are every time obliged to say "Those are not my units"? I'm referring to all the questions that we have been asking you. Doesn't that make you see that external neutral observers keep asking you the same question and you always answer, following your own logic, "They are not my units." But one must acknowledge that for an external observer, military man, UNPROFOR, a monitor, or in this case Mr. Akhavan, it's rather difficult. You have your own logic. You say, "I didn't give such orders. Those are not my units." But one must acknowledge that the military police, after all, was a part of the HVO, and you were the commander. How do you experience personally this constant contradiction? The crime was committed, you acknowledge that it is a crime, they say, "You ordered it," and you answer every time, "I did not order it." That is your right to say that. But you add, "But those are not my units." Does that mean that every time you repeated how they were not your units? How did you do it? You said, "I did not commit that crime and they are not my units," but it is very difficult for your interlocutor to understand that those were not your units. You repeated every time that the military police was reattached to you since the 16th of April, 11.42, but this was only for a specific assignment, and when the conflict stopped, et cetera, did you repeat that whole explanation every time or not?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I did not repeat that every time, Mr. President. That depended on the question of the interlocutor. I saw Mr. Akhavan for the first time then and the next time here in the courtroom. At the time, I didn't even know who he was except that he had come with another representative of the UN

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Did you say to yourself -- you don't need to answer this if you don't want to -- these same questions, did they bother you or not, the same questions being your units and you said, "They are not my units"? Did this bother you? Did this annoy you? After all, you were the commander of Central Bosnia. Every time you would say, "Yes, but on the 16th of April at 11.42, the military police," et cetera.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: There were many, many problems in evidence. When I was asked questions, I did my best to answer them as best I could under the conditions that existed. As far as I knew, I would give them my answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: We see already, and this will be visible every day, two or three people would come, one after another, with the same question, "Who committed the crime?" Let us make it quite clear. Did you name or identify the military police to anyone and did you explain this question of attachment as of 11.42 to anyone except here in court?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I did not ever mention to anyone except here in the courtroom what I said on the basis of my notes. Those people were unknown to me at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Is it normal for a commander to be confronted with a series of people he doesn't know and for that commander to enter into the internal problems of his army, the internal structure, and to present the dirty laundry, so to speak? Would that be normal for a commander to discuss these matters in public?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, these are usually internal affairs that are kept internal and are not discussed in public.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did you inform your superiors, your command, about those problems?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So Mr. Payam Akhavan appeared from somewhere, you don't know who he is, and what happens then? What did he say and what did you say?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: He was very angry after that. He started shouting, "Ahmici was in your area of responsibility," he kept repeating this, and he was perhaps irritated. I answered, "Yes, Ahmici is in my zone of responsibility, it is also in the zone of responsibility of the 3rd Corps," I told him that there was a conflict, and after that, that meeting ended.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: A man comes you never saw or heard of before, he comes to your command, you're a colonel, you're the commander of an Operative Zone, he yells at you, he accuses you. What was your reaction? How would Darko Kraljevic have reacted in such a case?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Just a moment, Mr. Nobilo. Judge Shahabuddeen has a question for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Let us go back a little to Colonel Stewart. Did you then think that Colonel Stewart was understanding you to mean that no elements of the HVO had participated in the commission of the crimes at Ahmici, whether or not they were under your command?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I believe that Colonel Stewart assumed that the HVO had participated in the crime in Ahmici because he showed me a list and a file claiming that the names were in there, the names of the perpetrators.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: I understand that you are saying to me what you think Colonel Stewart understood of the factual situation. I am asking you whether you then thought that he then had the impression that you were saying that no HVO elements had participated in the commission of those crimes?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I was clear in what I said to Colonel Stewart. I said "my" units, "my" HVO units did not commit the crime. I did not say to Colonel Stewart that no element of the HVO had committed it. I said "my" units, the units under my command had not committed the crime. That is what I said to him, and I believe that he was able to understand because he did discuss with me the structure of the HVO; in fact, I think that he was familiar with that structure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: General, you are quite consistent in your narrative of what you told Colonel Stewart. That is not my question. My question is: Did you then have the impression that whatever you told him, he understood you to mean that no HVO elements had participated in the commission of those crimes?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I think that he believed that some elements of the HVO had participated in the commission of the crime.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Mr. Nobilo, I wouldn't pursue it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Alas, you don't have a chance to put your question because my colleague Judge Rodrigues wishes to put a question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. General Blaskic, I should like to try and understand this question; that is, I should like to know whether, throughout those conversations and meetings, was there not a dialogue among the deaf because you kept saying to Thebault, to Stewart, to Akhavan, to de la Mota, "My units did not do those crimes." But the question is the following: Perhaps for you, you knew well that the military police were only attached to you; they were not a part of your units, they were not included in the concept of "my" units. But for the others, for Thebault, for Stewart, for Akhavan, for de la Mota, the military police was one of your units because it is normal, as we have seen here, it is normal for the military police to depend on you. In your opinion, at which point did you explain to all these people, "Wait, wait. It should be said my units didn't do it, and I wish to inform you that the military police is not a part of my unit"? Did they know this or not because you have already admitted here in this courtroom that it is not normal for the military police not to depend on the command of the Operative Zone. What do you think about that, General Blaskic? What is your impression? Was there a dialogue of the deaf or was your communication clear?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: There were people there who attended a meeting for the first time, Your Honour, and it is difficult for me to tell what prior knowledge they had about the HVO structure and everything else, but the dialogue between me and Colonel Stewart I believe was not a dialogue of the deaf, the more so as he knew the organisational structure of the HVO, he had it in his possession, at least a global organogram, and he was able to understand it. As for the other associates, it is hard for me to tell.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: I am sorry for interrupting you. So Bob Stewart knew well that the military police was not part of the structure of the HVO, that is, the military police was not included when you use the expression "my units"?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I assume that he knew. I never questioned Colonel Stewart to be able to say with certainty that he did know, but I believe he did know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: So, General, would you say the same of the other people, Thebault, Akhavan, and de la Mota, did they know?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Let me answer that in this way: Whatever questions they put to me in concrete terms, I tried to answer in the way the question was put. When they said that my units had done it, my association was that they meant units under my direct command. I don't know whether Akhavan and the others were familiar with the HVO structure. That I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Just a further point, Mr. Nobilo, but for Akhavan, for instance, what surprises me for Mr. Akhavan is that you didn't explain once again the same thing as Judge Rodrigues just said, and you said, "You know there was a conflict between the Bosnia army and us." You just said that, I think. It's in the transcript. I'm repeating it. But I'm sure you counsel are very vigilant in order to defend you properly. I have listened with interest to your answers to the questions of my colleague, but as regards Akhavan, if you pursued your logic, it seems to me that what you should have told Mr. Akhavan is not what you did tell him but simply, "Yes, since the 22nd of April, I think that HVO units committed this crime, but I wish to tell you that they are not under my responsibility." I don't have the transcript before me now, but I think Akhavan said to you -- you said to Akhavan, "I did not give orders for this crime to be committed, and there was a conflict between the BH army and the HVO." By giving such a reply, I think you provided doubt. You said that actually, the crime could have been committed just as well by the HVO as by the BH army. Let me summarise that slowly for the benefit of the interpreters. Let's me summarise once again. It seems to me that with regard to Mr. Akhavan, we are talking about the 4th of May, Ahmici took place almost a month before that, you knew, since the 22nd of April, in any event, Colonel Stewart persuaded you that there was considerable reason to believe that HVO units, and he thought they were your units, participated in that crime, and you yourself were convinced of that. I note with regard to Mr. Akhavan, when he said to you, "Your units under your orders killed civilians," your reply was, "I did not perpetrate that crime and, anyway, there was a conflict between the BH army and the HVO." So my question is the following: It seems to me that if you were faithful to your own logic, then you should have said, "Yes, I think that HVO units most probably did participate in the commission of that crime. I wish to tell you that as far as I'm concerned, I did not give any such orders and those units are not subordinated to me on the operational level." Do you understand my question?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Mr. President, I do understand the question, but never did I say to Mr. Akhavan that the crime was committed by units of the BH army. I got an interpretation to that effect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes. You didn't say that, but you said that, "You see, there's a conflict between the Bosnian army and the HVO." At least that's the interpretation that I received. It seems to me that the 4th of May, according to the answer you gave to Judge Rodrigues and to Judge Shahabuddeen, it seems to me that ever since the 22nd of April, in your conscience at least, and today also you're fully conscious and eager to discover the truth, since the 22nd of April you tell us you were not formally convinced because there was no commission of inquiry, but still you had serious suspicions regarding the military police. At least, Colonel Stewart really distressed you, and to Akhavan, you said, "But there was a conflict between the BH army and the HVO. I did not perpetrate that crime," whereas in substance, it seems to me that following the logic of what you have told us, it would have been simpler for you to say, "Yes. First, an investigation needs to be conducted. Second, I think that there is a probability that a unit which apparently belongs to the HVO is behind it," and then repeat once again, "But you see, I'm the operational commander but not for all the units." So can you help me in providing an answer to this, after which we shall break, except if Mr. Nobilo has a question to put, and as the Defence is always the last to speak, we will give him a chance to do so. Do you understand why I am asking you this question following the questions of my colleagues?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Mr. President, I shall try.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Maybe you can answer tomorrow. I don't mind. Perhaps you're too tired. Perhaps you can answer tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I'll try to answer it now. I'd rather not leave it for tomorrow. Akhavan said to me literally this: "Your units, under your orders, committed a massacre in Ahmici." That was his allegation, and to this allegation I answered, "Upon my orders they did not commit the crime. I did not order the crime. I know for certain that my unit did not commit it." And this was my first encounter with this person. I saw him for the first time then. Until I came here to the Tribunal, I never met him again, as far as I can remember, and judging by my notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Just one question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Nobilo, you are entitled to put your question. We interrupted you, and if the interpreters can bear with us a few more minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Nobilo, proceed with your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: It has to do with the very substance of the matter you have raised. General, an unknown person, you don't know who he is, and he accuses you personally of having ordered a crime in your area of responsibility, in an area in which you have several thousand soldiers. You told him what you did. How would he have fared in any other command in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I could tell you. I assume that would have been his last visit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I didn't hear the end. Just a moment, please. I didn't get the end of it. Could you repeat the sentence? "That would have been his last visit"? Very well. That is the last question from the Defence. It is 6.10, and we're going to break to resume tomorrow morning. We have to have a hearing that we missed. That is why we're going to work normally tomorrow, from 10:00 to 1.00, and from 2.30 to 5.30. The hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, according to the plan that we received, only the afternoon hearing was planned for tomorrow. Is this a change, according to the schedule we received, Mr. Dubuisson?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, there is a change. Perhaps we were not specific enough. Maybe I wasn't quite clear.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: No, we're making up for last Wednesday. It was decided at the end of last week that we make up for this Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Does it bother you to have a hearing tomorrow morning? It is to make up lost time. Is that acceptable? It is up to you to choose. I don't mind either way.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: We gladly accept the time, but this is the first time we've heard of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Maybe I did not explain it well. Maybe it's the dialogue of the deaf, as Judge Rodrigues mentioned a moment ago, so I apologise. General Blaskic, do you agree for tomorrow morning? Will you be ready for tomorrow morning?

utterances.speaker: TIHOMIR BLASKIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. Tomorrow morning at 10.00 a.m. The hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: at 6.10 p.m., to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 17th day of March, 1999, at 10.00 a.m. 25
